meaning: to have to start again from the beginning after a plan or idea has failed
example: The experiment failed again, so we are back to the drawing board.
origin: Likely from architects and engineers who returned to their drawing boards to redesign plans after a failed design; the exact origin is uncertain

wrong_meanings.meaning: to make a detailed picture of a finished design
wrong_meanings.why_wrong: This describes drawing, but the idiom refers to restarting after a failure, not to producing a finished picture.
The idiom describes failure and starting again, so it is the opposite of a success.

wrong_meanings.meaning: to give up on a project permanently
wrong_meanings.why_wrong: The idiom implies starting again, not abandoning the project for good.

explanation: 'Back to the drawing board' means that an attempt has failed and the work must begin again from the start. It is often used in research, design and science when results do not support a hypothesis.
